practice_questions.text: State what is meant by homeostasis.

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of a synapse in the transmission of a nerve impulse.
practice_questions.marks: When an impulse reaches the end of a neurone, neurotransmitters are released into the synaptic gap (1). These chemicals diffuse across and bind to receptors on the next neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the myelin sheath helps nerve impulses travel efficiently.
practice_questions.marks: The myelin sheath is a fatty/insulating layer around the axon (1). It prevents the electrical impulse from being lost to surrounding tissue (1). This means impulses travel faster along myelinated neurones (1).

practice_questions.text: Compare the roles of sensory neurones and motor neurones in a reflex arc.
practice_questions.marks: Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS (1). Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors (1). Both transmit electrical impulses (1). However, they carry signals in opposite directions — sensory towards the CNS, motor away from it (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why reflex actions are important for survival. Use an example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6 marks): Full explanation with a named example, correct reflex arc pathway, and clear link to survival. Secure (3–4 marks): Correct pathway with partial explanation of survival advantage. Developing (1–2 marks): Basic idea that reflexes are fast/automatic. Example points: Reflexes are automatic/involuntary responses (1). They do not involve conscious thought so are very fast (1). Example: touching a hot object — receptor detects heat, impulse travels via sensory neurone to relay neurone in spinal cord, then motor neurone to muscle (effector), hand pulled away (1). The brain is bypassed so response is faster (1). This protects the body from harm/damage (1). Speed of response reduces injury (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the three components of a homeostatic control system.
practice_questions.marks: Receptors detect changes in the environment/stimulus (1). Coordination centres (brain/spinal cord) process the information (1). Effectors (muscles/glands) carry out the response (1). Any two for 2 marks.

practice_questions.marks: Hormones are secreted directly into the bloodstream (1). They are carried in the blood to target organs where they have their effect (1).

before.content_html:
The Menstrual Cycle

The menstrual cycle is a roughly 28-day process controlled by hormones. It prepares the female body for pregnancy each month. If the released egg is not fertilised, the lining of the uterus is shed during menstruation (a period), and the cycle begins again.

The cycle has four main stages. Days 1–5: Menstruation occurs — the uterus lining breaks down and is shed. Days 6–13: The uterus lining begins to rebuild and thicken. Day 14: Ovulation occurs — a mature egg is released from one of the ovaries. Days 15–28: The uterus lining is maintained, ready for a fertilised egg to implant. If no fertilisation occurs, the cycle starts again.

Hormones Controlling the Menstrual Cycle

Four hormones interact to control the menstrual cycle. FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) is released by the pituitary gland. It causes an egg to mature inside a follicle in the ovary and stimulates the ovaries to produce oestrogen.

Oestrogen is produced by the ovaries. It causes the uterus lining to thicken and repair after menstruation. Rising oestrogen levels also stimulate the pituitary gland to release a surge of LH (luteinising hormone). LH triggers ovulation around day 14.

Key Fact

FSH matures the egg and stimulates oestrogen production. Oestrogen thickens the uterus lining and triggers LH release. LH triggers ovulation. Progesterone maintains the uterus lining after ovulation and inhibits FSH and LH.

After ovulation, the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum and produces progesterone. Progesterone maintains the thick uterus lining so that a fertilised egg can implant. It also inhibits FSH and LH, preventing another egg from maturing. If no fertilisation occurs, the corpus luteum breaks down, progesterone levels drop, and the uterus lining is shed — beginning menstruation and the next cycle.

The hormones of the menstrual cycle interact through feedback loops. Oestrogen produced by the developing follicle stimulates LH release (a positive feedback effect). After ovulation, progesterone from the corpus luteum inhibits both FSH and LH (negative feedback), preventing a second egg from being released. When progesterone falls, FSH is no longer inhibited, so the cycle restarts.

Contraception

Contraception prevents pregnancy. Methods fall into two main categories: hormonal contraception and barrier methods.

Hormonal methods work by releasing hormones that interfere with the menstrual cycle. The combined pill contains oestrogen and progesterone — it prevents ovulation and thickens cervical mucus so sperm cannot pass through easily. The progesterone-only pill (mini-pill) mainly thickens cervical mucus. Other options include contraceptive injections, implants and intrauterine devices (IUDs) that release hormones.

Barrier methods physically block sperm from reaching the egg. Condoms (male and female) also protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Diaphragms cover the cervix and are used with spermicide. Barrier methods have no hormonal side effects but must be used correctly every time.

Hormonal methods are very effective at preventing pregnancy when used correctly but can have side effects such as headaches, mood changes or blood clots. They do not protect against STIs. Barrier methods are less effective at preventing pregnancy but condoms are the only method that protects against STIs. The choice of contraception depends on reliability, side effects, convenience and whether STI protection is needed.

Key Fact

Hormonal contraception is highly effective at preventing pregnancy but does not protect against STIs and can have side effects. Barrier methods (e.g. condoms) protect against STIs but are less effective at preventing pregnancy.

Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART)

Some couples have difficulty conceiving naturally. ART includes treatments that help people become pregnant.

IVF (in vitro fertilisation) involves giving the mother FSH and LH to stimulate multiple eggs to mature. The eggs are collected and fertilised with sperm in a laboratory. Fertilised embryos develop for a few days before one or two are transferred to the mother’s uterus. IVF is effective but expensive, physically demanding and has a relatively low success rate per cycle.

Clomifene therapy is a fertility drug. It works by stimulating the release of FSH and LH from the pituitary gland, which triggers ovulation. It is less invasive and cheaper than IVF, though it can increase the chance of multiple pregnancies.

Key Fact

IVF involves stimulating egg production with FSH/LH, collecting eggs, fertilising them with sperm in a lab, and transferring embryos to the uterus. Clomifene therapy stimulates ovulation by triggering FSH and LH release.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'variation'.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark:
• The differences in characteristics between individuals of the same species (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe two sources of genetic variation in a population.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks (any two from):
• Mutations cause random changes in DNA / can produce new alleles (1)
• Sexual reproduction mixes alleles from two parents (1)
• Meiosis produces gametes with different combinations of alleles (1)
• Random fertilisation creates unique offspring (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain how natural selection leads to evolution in a population.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Individuals show variation in characteristics (1)
• Those best suited to the environment are more likely to survive and reproduce (1)
• They pass on the alleles for advantageous characteristics to offspring, so over generations the allele becomes more common / the population evolves (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain how the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria provides evidence for Darwin's theory of natural selection.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Random mutation in a bacterium gives resistance to an antibiotic (1)
• When the antibiotic is used, non-resistant bacteria are killed but the resistant one survives and reproduces (1)
• The resistance allele is passed to offspring, so the resistant strain becomes more common / this shows natural selection in action (1)

practice_questions.text: Compare natural selection and selective breeding.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Natural selection is driven by the environment / selective breeding is driven by humans (1)
• Both involve organisms with certain characteristics being more likely to reproduce (1)
• Natural selection takes many generations / selective breeding can produce rapid changes (1)
• Selective breeding reduces genetic variation in the population / natural selection maintains or increases it (1)

practice_questions.text: A species of beetle lives on an island. A volcanic eruption splits the island in two, separating the beetle population. Explain how this could eventually lead to two new species of beetle.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Clear explanation covering geographic isolation, different environmental conditions on each island, different selection pressures favouring different characteristics, allele frequencies changing over generations, and eventually the two populations becoming so different they can no longer interbreed — speciation.

Secure (3–4 marks): Explains that the populations are separated and experience different conditions leading to different characteristics, with some reference to natural selection and becoming different species.

Developing (1–2 marks): Identifies that the populations are separated and may become different, but lacks detail about the mechanism of natural selection or speciation.

lessons.title: Trophic Levels, Pyramids & the Carbon Cycle

before.content_html:
Trophic Levels and Food Chains

In any ecosystem, energy flows from the Sun through living organisms. The position an organism occupies in a food chain is called its trophic level. Every food chain begins with a producer — an organism (usually a green plant or alga) that converts light energy into chemical energy through photosynthesis.

Organisms that eat producers are called primary consumers (trophic level 2). Those that eat primary consumers are secondary consumers (trophic level 3). Tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers and sit at trophic level 4 or above.

Key Fact

Trophic levels: Level 1 = Producers (plants) → Level 2 = Primary consumers (herbivores) → Level 3 = Secondary consumers (carnivores) → Level 4 = Tertiary consumers (top predators). Energy is transferred along the chain but decreases at each level.

Pyramids of Biomass

A pyramid of biomass represents the total mass of living material at each trophic level. The producer level always forms the widest bar at the bottom, and each successive level is narrower. This is because energy is lost at every trophic level, so less biomass can be supported higher up the food chain.

Energy is lost between trophic levels through several processes: organisms use energy for movement and other life processes; energy is lost as heat during respiration; and not all parts of an organism are eaten (bones, shells, roots). As a result, only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is passed to the next.

Unlike pyramids of numbers (which can sometimes be inverted, for example when a single large tree supports many insects), pyramids of biomass are almost always a true pyramid shape. This is because they show the total mass of organisms, not just how many there are. Since energy is lost at each transfer, the total biomass decreases at each trophic level, regardless of the number or size of individual organisms.

This also explains why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels — by the fifth level, so little energy remains that it cannot support a viable population of top predators.

Material Cycles — Why Recycling Matters

The materials that living organisms are made from are constantly recycled between the living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) parts of an ecosystem. When organisms die, decomposers (mainly bacteria and fungi) break down the dead material. This releases nutrients back into the soil and gases back into the atmosphere, where they can be used again by other organisms. Without decomposition, essential elements would remain locked up in dead organisms and would eventually run out.

The Carbon Cycle

The carbon cycle describes how carbon moves between the atmosphere, living organisms, and the environment. It is one of the most important material cycles because carbon is the basis of all organic molecules.

The key processes in the carbon cycle are:

Photosynthesis — producers remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and convert it into glucose (organic compounds). This is the main way carbon enters living systems.

Respiration — all living organisms (plants, animals, and microorganisms) carry out respiration, releasing carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere. The equation: $$\text{glucose} + \text{oxygen} \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water}$$

Feeding — carbon passes along food chains when animals eat plants or other animals.

Decomposition — when organisms die, decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down the organic matter. The decomposers respire, returning carbon dioxide to the atmosphere. This is a critical role of microorganisms in the carbon cycle.

Combustion — burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) releases carbon dioxide that was locked away millions of years ago, increasing atmospheric CO₂ levels.

Key Fact

Carbon enters living systems through photosynthesis and returns to the atmosphere through respiration, decomposition, and combustion. Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) play a vital role by breaking down dead matter and respiring, returning carbon to the cycle.

The Water Cycle

The water cycle describes how water moves continuously between the Earth's surface and the atmosphere. The main processes are: Evaporation — water from oceans, lakes, and rivers is heated by the Sun and turns into water vapour. Transpiration — plants release water vapour from their leaves. Condensation — water vapour cools as it rises and condenses into tiny droplets, forming clouds. Precipitation — water falls as rain, snow, or hail. The water then collects in rivers, lakes, and oceans, or soaks into the ground.

In areas of drought, potable water (safe drinking water) can be produced by desalination — removing salt from seawater. This can be done by distillation (boiling and condensing) or reverse osmosis (forcing water through a membrane). Desalination is effective but requires a lot of energy, making it expensive.

Plants need nitrates from the soil to make amino acids and proteins. But plants cannot use nitrogen gas (N₂) directly from the atmosphere. Nitrates are made available to plants in three main ways:

1. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria — these live freely in the soil or in root nodules of leguminous plants (peas, beans, clover). They convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia, which is then converted to nitrates by other bacteria. 2. Decomposition and nitrifying bacteria — when organisms die, decomposers break down proteins into ammonia. Nitrifying bacteria then convert ammonia into nitrites and then into nitrates that plants can absorb. 3. Fertilisers — farmers add artificial fertilisers containing nitrates directly to the soil. Crop rotation with leguminous plants also helps — the nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their root nodules enrich the soil with nitrates for the next crop.

Denitrifying bacteria do the reverse — they convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas, which is released into the atmosphere. This completes the cycle but can reduce soil fertility.

Key Fact

Nitrates are made available for plants through: 1. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (in soil or legume root nodules). 2. Decomposers + nitrifying bacteria converting dead matter → ammonia → nitrates. 3. Adding fertilisers or using crop rotation with legumes.

When describing the carbon cycle, always mention the role of microorganisms as decomposers. Decomposers don't just break things down; they also respire, which is what actually returns carbon dioxide to the atmosphere. Many students forget this second step. Also remember that combustion of fossil fuels is a human addition to the cycle that increases atmospheric CO₂.

glossary_terms.definition: The level at which an organism feeds in a food chain. Level 1 = producers, Level 2 = primary consumers, Level 3 = secondary consumers.
An organism that makes its own food using energy from the Sun through photosynthesis, such as green plants and algae.
The process by which green plants and algae use light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.
Animals that eat producers (plants). Also called herbivores. Occupy trophic level 2.
Animals that eat primary consumers. Occupy trophic level 3.
Animals at the top of the food chain with no natural predators. Occupy trophic level 4 or above.
A diagram that shows the total mass of living material (biomass) at each trophic level of a food chain.
The total dry mass of all the organisms at a particular trophic level.
Organisms (mainly bacteria and fungi) that break down dead organic matter, releasing nutrients back into the soil and gases into the atmosphere.
The biogeochemical cycle by which carbon moves between the atmosphere, living organisms, the ocean, and the Earth's crust.
The chemical process in living cells that releases energy from glucose, producing carbon dioxide as a waste product.
Non-renewable energy sources formed from the remains of ancient organisms over millions of years, including coal, oil, and natural gas.
The continuous movement of water between the Earth's surface and the atmosphere through evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection.
Water that is safe to drink, containing low levels of dissolved salts and microorganisms.
The process of removing salt from seawater to produce fresh drinking water, usually by distillation or reverse osmosis.
Mineral ions containing nitrogen that plants absorb from the soil and use to make amino acids and proteins.
Bacteria in the soil that convert ammonia into nitrites and then into nitrates, making nitrogen available for plant uptake.
Bacteria that convert nitrates in the soil back into nitrogen gas, which is released into the atmosphere.
